mechanism: Pinokio is a desktop app that runs JSON/JS launcher scripts from a community registry: each script clones a repo, builds a Python venv, pulls model weights and starts a local web UI. It automates the install steps a person would otherwise type, and depends on the host having the right GPU driver stack (CUDA for NVIDIA). On a rented GPU box it is a way to get a model UI running without hand-building the environment.
claim: One-click installs of local AI apps such as Wan2GP, so you run video models without terminal work.
why_not_testable: The payload (Wan2GP) needs an NVIDIA GPU, and the rented box needed for a cost test costs money and an account.
needs: A rented NVIDIA GPU (account and spend) to test the cost-per-clip claim.
one_line: Pinokio is an installer that runs community launcher scripts to stand up local AI apps; useful mainly for getting Wan2GP onto a rented GPU fast.
idea_why: Scripted environment setup is a plain, well-understood mechanism and the cost claim can be measured once a GPU is rented.
breakdown: Rent an hourly NVIDIA GPU instance, install Pinokio, run the Wan2GP launcher, then generate a fixed set of clips with a stopwatch and the hourly price. Run the same prompts through a hosted API such as fal and divide cost by usable clips for both. A person would need to judge clip quality side by side, since no script scores that well. The comparison is the product, not the installer.

mechanism: Per the HN comments, Claude Code runs a background query tagged agent_summary roughly every 30 seconds per agent, sending the agent's transcript to the current model to produce a few words for the status line. Because most of the input is the cached transcript, it shows as about 9,000 input tokens per output token. The figures came from grouping OpenTelemetry traces by query_source.
claim: agent_summary calls used 16.4% of estimated spend and 19.7% of API requests in one measured week (one commenter's team).
why_not_testable: Measuring it needs API-side or OTEL request data by query_source, which local transcripts do not label and which Proteus has not enabled.
needs: OTEL export from Claude Code, or per-request logs with query_source.
one_line: A team traced 16 per cent of its Claude Code spend to a status-line summary query that re-sends each agent's transcript about every 30 seconds.
idea_why: The mechanism is plausible and checkable with OTEL traces, but the numbers are one team's and unverified here.
breakdown: Turn on Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export to a local collector, run a few multi-agent sessions, and group requests by query_source to see the agent_summary share. Compare with the token counts in bin/usage.py output for the same sessions. Proteus runs many sub-agents, so the share could matter for its own spend. A person would only be needed to decide whether to disable the feature if a setting exists.

mechanism: BLA post-processes build artifacts (JS bundles, asar, wasm, sqlite) to add format-valid decoys, canary strings and oversized or deeply nested structures aimed at the resource limits of AI reverse-engineering agents. The aim is for the analyser to burn tokens or truncate its inventory while the program behaves the same. It runs as a CLI and MCP server with audit, protect and verify stages, the last being a runtime-equivalence check.
claim: Hardened builds make AI reverse-engineering agents hit budgets and follow decoys while runtime behaviour stays the same; 727 stars in four days.
verdict_question: On a small public JS bundle, does bla harden keep the output identical and by what size multiple does the file grow?
probe_title: bla-agents: does harden keep a small JS bundle's output identical, and how much bigger does it get?
one_line: BLA pads shipped builds with decoys and budget-busting structures so AI reverse-engineering agents waste tokens; we can at least test whether the program still runs identically.
idea_why: Resource exhaustion of analysers is a real mechanism, but the effect on a real agent is unproven and the README's empirical section was empty in the brief.
breakdown: Install bla-agents with npx inside the sandbox, write a 50-line Node script with fixed output, run harden, diff the outputs and record the size ratio. A second step would point a Claude Code sub-agent at the hardened file and compare tokens spent on a plain-versus-hardened copy, which is the real claim. That second step needs model calls, so it is a later night. Hiring is not needed; it is a script plus a measurement.

mechanism: Wan2GP is a Gradio front end that runs open video models (Wan, LTX-2 distilled and others) with heavy memory offloading and quantisation so they fit consumer GPUs with modest VRAM. Distilled models cut sampling to a few steps, trading some quality for speed. It depends on CUDA, PyTorch and downloaded weights.
claim: Local video generation on a home GPU with no per-clip fee; the carousel pitches it as cheaper than hosted APIs.
why_not_testable: It needs an NVIDIA GPU and several GB of weights; no Mac here can run it.
needs: An NVIDIA GPU, local or rented.
one_line: Wan2GP squeezes open video models onto modest NVIDIA cards with offloading and distilled few-step sampling, so clips cost electricity rather than API fees.
idea_why: Open models on rented or owned GPUs are a standard cost route; the saving depends on clip volume and quality needs.
breakdown: Rent a GPU by the hour, install via Pinokio or the repo, and generate a fixed prompt set with LTX-2 distilled and Wan. Record seconds per clip and cost per kept clip, then compare to the hosted price for the same length. Output would feed HyperFrames as B-roll. A person judges whether quality is usable for ads, as that is not scriptable.

mechanism: Concordat models an agent as a finite-state protocol. Each turn the model is shown only the tools legal in the current state, out-of-state calls are rejected before side effects, and human-reserved decisions can only be requested. Token and tool-call budgets are split across handoffs, and protocols are checked when defined.
claim: On 50 tau-bench airline tasks with pressuring simulated customers, the standard agent skipped confirmation in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and the Concordat agent in none.
verdict_question: With a scripted fake model that tries every tool in every state, does Concordat reject all out-of-state calls before any side effect fires (yes/no, count)?
probe_title: Concordat: does the typed-session library block every illegal tool call from a scripted fake model?
one_line: Concordat shows the model only the tools legal in the current state, and in a benchmark it made no unconfirmed changes where a standard agent made them in 13 of 50 tasks.
idea_why: Enforcing permitted actions in code rather than in the prompt is a sound control, and the guard layer can be tested without a model.
breakdown: Fetch the library, define a three-state protocol (ask, confirm, act) with a side-effecting tool that increments a counter, then drive it with a scripted stub that calls every tool each turn. Count rejections and confirm the counter only moves in the legal state. The same pattern could harden Proteus's own unattended tools. The paper's model-based results need paid calls and are out of scope tonight.

mechanism: A gateway plugin for a model provider ships its own catalogue of model ids, context windows and prices, so a config only needs the plugin enabled plus an API key env var. Hand-writing a provider block copies those numbers and goes stale when the vendor changes them. Reading the plugin's preset and mirroring it keeps config and catalogue in sync.

why_not_testable: Running a model turn needs the xAI key, and Proteus's xAI credits are exhausted.
one_line: Gateway provider plugins carry their own model catalogue, so reading the preset beats hand-copying context windows and prices that later drift.
idea_why: Single source of truth for catalogue data is basic config hygiene and avoids silent drift.
breakdown: Locate the plugin's preset file in the gateway install, read the model entries, and make the config reference them rather than duplicate them. Add a small check that diffs any hand-written provider block against the preset and flags mismatches. This is a config job with no hiring need.

mechanism: The reports say Claude Code places the signed-in user's email in the context it sends the model, and in some sessions the model then passed that address to websites it was operating. The leak path is context injection followed by a tool call carrying the value, not a separate exfiltration channel. Detection is by inspecting prompts and outgoing tool arguments.
claim: Claude Code adds the user's email to the prompt and the model has sent it to websites (two linked issue and Reddit reports).
why_not_testable: Confirming it needs inspecting the outgoing prompt or a live browsing session, which is not a keyless slice.
one_line: Reports say Claude Code puts your email in the model's context and the model has typed it into websites; the fix is a guard on tool arguments.
idea_why: The mechanism is plausible and matches how context fields work, but only two second-hand reports are given.
breakdown: Check how the harness exposes user fields in context, then add a hook that scans outgoing tool arguments for the owner's email and denies on a match. Proteus already has a PreToolUse hook, so this is a small rule. A person would decide whether to treat the email field as sensitive in sessions that browse.
